articleHeadline: Why leptospirosis remains a serious threat long after people wade through contaminated water
articleSummary: Leptospirosis, caused by Leptospira bacteria excreted in rodent urine, remains a serious threat during the rainy season and floods. Transmission mainly occurs when wading through floodwaters contaminated by rat urine; less common routes include contaminated food or undercooked meat. Incubation is typically 5–14 days (range 2–30). Most infections are mild, but a substantial portion progresses to severe leptospirosis, which can be rapidly fatal. Early symptoms include fever, myalgia (calf muscles), fatigue, headache, and conjunctival suffusion; severe disease features jaundice, reduced urine output, dark urine, abdominal pain, and shortness of breath, with pulmonary hemorrhage and bleeding possible. Prophylaxis with doxycycline near exposure may reduce risk; timing is critical, and dosing varies with skin integrity and exposure. Contraindications include pregnancy and children under 12; alternatives exist. Mild cases respond to oral antibiotics; severe cases require IV antibiotics and may need dialysis; Weil’s disease carries high mortality.

Wear protective clothing, camp in open, ventilated areas, and seek swift care if fever or joint pain and rash appear after outdoor activities.

articleHeadline: Scientists use mining data to build malaria alert system in Amazon
articleSummary: Malaria in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory in the Brazilian Amazon dropped after expelling illegal miners (garimpeiros). articleSummary: On 2 September 2026, in Gollaguppa village of Polavaram district, Andhra Pradesh, 71 residents were given chloroquine tablets to prevent malaria.
